title: Kashkari Warns Inflation Is Too High Across 'All Aspects' of Economy
excerpt: In a Sunday interview, the Minneapolis Fed president said price pressures have spread far beyond oil into services, backing more rate hikes — while admitting rates can't fix the Strait of Hormuz.
body:
• Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari told Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures" that U.S. inflation is too high across all sectors, not just energy: strip out volatile energy and food, he said, and "inflation is still too high."
  • He warned that price pressures have spread into the services sector and everyday costs: "The inflation that the American people are feeling every day is much beyond just oil prices."
  • Kashkari backed last week's unanimous quarter-point hike to 3.75%–4.00% and was one of three officials who dissented in favor of a hike at the prior meeting.
  • His comments echoed Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who estimated August inflation at about 3.6% on the Fed's preferred gauge; rate-futures markets price roughly a two-in-three chance of another hike this year.

Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Neel Kashkari said Sunday that U.S. inflation remains too high across "all aspects" of the economy, warning that price pressures have spread well beyond the oil shock from the widening Middle East conflict into services and the everyday costs households face.

"So even if we strip out energy, which is really volatile, and strip out food — they matter a lot — but in terms of where the economy is going, inflation is still too high," Kashkari told Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures" program, according to Reuters. "We're going to do our part, and then hopefully we will get some help from other sectors of the economy, as things go back to normal."

The Fed's most persistent hawk speaks

Kashkari has been the Federal Open Market Committee's leading hawk for months. He supported last week's unanimous vote to raise the benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to 3.75%–4.00% — the first U.S. rate hike since July 2023. At the prior meeting he was one of three officials to dissent in favor of a hike when the majority opted to leave rates unchanged, arguing that waiting too long risked entrenching inflation and forcing even more aggressive measures later.

His Sunday remarks echoed the case Fed Chair Kevin Warsh made after Wednesday's decision. Warsh estimated that inflation on the gauge the Fed uses for its 2% target was likely around 3.6% in August, a figure that will not be released officially until later this month. Projections released alongside the rate decision showed all but two policymakers expect at least one more quarter-point increase this year.

"The inflation that the American people are feeling every day is much beyond just oil prices. It's in all aspects of the economy. It's in the services sector, for example, widely. So we have tools to bring that back down."

— Neel Kashkari, President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

What rates can — and can't — fix

Kashkari drew a sharp line between inflation the Fed can fight and the part it cannot. Crude prices have soared as hostilities intensified between the U.S. and Iran, with oil tankers attacked and sunk in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia closing its vital East-West pipeline after aerial attacks. The Fed's job, he said, is to get inflation back to the 2% target — and there is nothing interest rates can do to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or bring down oil prices. "Hopefully, we'll get some help from other parts of government or other parts of the real economy," he added.

The distinction matters for households. Energy-driven inflation can fade on its own if supply routes reopen; services inflation — rent, health care, dining out, insurance — tends to stick, and it is where Kashkari sees the real danger. That is also the inflation most sensitive to Fed policy, and it is why markets heard his interview as a signal that the hiking cycle is not done. Rate-futures markets now reflect about a two-in-three chance the policy rate ends 2026 in the 4.00%–4.25% range, with a strong likelihood of climbing at least another quarter point by mid-2027.

Diaspora angle

Kashkari is one of the most prominent Indian-Americans in U.S. economic policymaking, and his outspoken hawkishness has made him a closely watched voice well beyond central-banking circles. For diaspora families balancing mortgages, small-business borrowing and education costs, his message translates into plain arithmetic: expect borrowing costs to stay elevated, and plan accordingly.

What's next

The next read on the Fed's preferred inflation gauge arrives later this month, when the official August figure is released and Warsh's 3.6% estimate gets its test. After that, attention turns to the next FOMC meeting and whether services inflation cools enough to let the committee pause — or confirms Kashkari's case for more hikes.
